result: Expectation suppression in the ventral visual stream (V1, LOC, TOFC) is present only when stimuli are attended, and vanishes when attention is directed away from the predictable objects. This attention-dependent modulation was statistically confirmed by significant expectation-by-attention interactions across all three ROIs, with Bayesian analyses providing moderate support for the absence of expectation suppression when objects were unattended.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 demonstrate robust expectation suppression in V1, LOC, and TOFC when objects are attended (all p≤0.001), while C13-C15 show absence of suppression when unattended (all p>0.4). Claims C16-C18 provide Bayesian evidence (BF10<0.2) supporting the null hypothesis of no suppression when unattended. Claims C19-C21 confirm significant interactions (all p≤0.009), demonstrating the robustness of the attention-dependent pattern. Whole-brain analyses (C60, C61, C64) corroborate these ROI findings across the entire ventral visual stream.

result: Expectation suppression exhibits stimulus specificity in higher visual areas (LOC and TOFC), where suppression is significantly larger in stimulus-driven than non-stimulus-driven voxels. In contrast, V1 shows stimulus-unspecific suppression, with no significant difference between stimulus-driven and non-stimulus-driven voxels, suggesting different suppression mechanisms across the visual hierarchy.
evaluation: Claims C22-C23 demonstrate significant stimulus specificity in LOC (p=3.4e-4) and TOFC (p=5.1e-5), while C24-C25 show no such difference in V1 (p=0.298, BF10=0.307 supporting null). Claim C70 confirms all subpopulations show suppression (p<0.05), supporting the interpretation in C71-C72 that V1 exhibits general suppression while higher areas show selective, stimulus-specific suppression. The statistical evidence is robust and the interpretation is well-supported by the data pattern.

result: Pupil dilation is significantly larger for unexpected compared to expected stimuli when objects are attended, with the difference emerging ~600ms after stimulus onset and reaching significance between 1.5-2.8s. However, no significant pupil dilation difference is observed when objects are unattended, and the interaction between attention conditions is not statistically reliable.
evaluation: Claims C26-C28 provide clear evidence for pupil dilation differences when objects are attended (pcluster=0.017), with specific temporal dynamics. Claim C29 shows absence of significant differences when unattended (all p>0.05), though C30 indicates the interaction is not reliable (p=0.393). The statistical evidence supports the main finding of attention-dependent pupil responses to expectation violations, though the lack of significant interaction suggests caution in interpreting the difference between conditions.

result: When objects are attended, expectation suppression in V1 is positively correlated with pupil dilation differences between unexpected and expected stimuli, suggesting a link between neural suppression and arousal-related pupil responses. This association is not reliable in LOC or TOFC, and is absent across all ROIs when objects are unattended.
evaluation: Claim C31 demonstrates a significant correlation in V1 when attended (p=0.019, dz=0.436), while C32-C33 show no reliable association in LOC or TOFC (both p>0.16, BF10<0.47). Claims C34-C36 confirm absence of correlation when unattended across all ROIs (all p>0.86, BF10<0.2). The pattern is consistent and statistically supported, though the specificity to V1 and the moderate effect size suggest this mechanism may be one of several contributing to expectation suppression.

result: Expectations facilitate behavioral performance during object categorization, with participants showing significantly faster and more accurate responses to expected compared to unexpected stimuli. No such behavioral benefit is observed during the character categorization task when objects are unattended. Both tasks showed similar overall difficulty levels.
evaluation: Claims C37-C38 demonstrate significant behavioral benefits when objects are attended (accuracy: p=3.2e-4, RT: p=3.8e-9), while C39-C40 show no benefits when unattended (both p>0.1, BF10<0.6). Claims C75-C77 confirm similar task difficulty (accuracy ~94%, RT difference ~28ms), ruling out differential task engagement as a confound. The behavioral data strongly support that expectations facilitate performance only when stimuli are attended, paralleling the neural findings.

result: When objects are attended, larger expectation suppression in V1 and TOFC is associated with greater behavioral RT benefits from expectations. No such association is found in LOC when attended, or in any ROI when objects are unattended.
evaluation: Claims C41-C42 show significant correlations in V1 (p=0.020) and TOFC (p=0.032) when attended, while C43 shows no reliable correlation in LOC (p=0.176, BF10=0.439). Claim C44 confirms absence of associations when unattended (all p>0.67, BF10<0.2). The evidence supports a link between neural and behavioral effects of expectations in specific regions, though the lack of overall interaction effects and the selective pattern across ROIs suggests the relationship is complex.

result: Participants demonstrated above-chance explicit knowledge of object pair associations for both attended and unattended image sets in the post-scanning recognition task, with no significant difference in accuracy or reaction time between the two sets. This indicates that statistical regularities were learned equally well regardless of attention condition during the main task.
evaluation: Claims C45-C46 show above-chance performance for both attended (62.1%, p=4.6e-8) and unattended (58.7%, p=2.2e-4) sets. Claims C47-C48 demonstrate no significant differences between sets in accuracy (p=0.256, BF10=0.737) or RT (p=0.236, BF10=0.358). This evidence effectively rules out differential learning as an explanation for the absence of expectation suppression when objects were unattended, strengthening the main conclusion that attention gates the expression of learned expectations.

result: Object identity can be decoded above chance from neural activity patterns in V1, LOC, and TOFC regardless of whether objects are attended or unattended, with no significant differences in decoding accuracy between attention conditions. This demonstrates that object-specific visual processing continues even when objects are not attended.
evaluation: Claims C49-C53 demonstrate above-chance decoding across ROIs and attention conditions (all p≤0.002), except C54 for TOFC when attended (p=0.143, BF10=0.388). Claims C55-C57 show no significant differences between attention conditions (all p>0.09, BF10<0.7). This evidence effectively rules out the alternative explanation that unattended objects were not processed, supporting the interpretation that attention specifically gates predictive processing rather than sensory processing per se. The one exception (TOFC attended) may reflect noise or task-related factors.

result: Expectation suppression in non-sensory areas (anterior insula, frontal and parietal cortex) is only observed when predictions are task-relevant, while expectation suppression in the ventral visual stream persists regardless of task relevance as long as stimuli are attended. This dissociation suggests different functional roles for expectation effects in sensory versus non-sensory regions.
evaluation: Claims C62-C63 identify non-sensory clusters showing expectation suppression only when objects are attended and categorized. Claims C67-C69 demonstrate through conjunction analysis that only ventral visual stream shows suppression across both task-relevant and task-irrelevant conditions. This dissociation is well-supported by the data and provides important insights into the functional specificity of expectation effects, suggesting non-sensory regions reflect task-related processes (e.g., response inhibition, decision-making) rather than perceptual predictions per se.

result: Pupil dilation is positively associated with BOLD responses in V1 across all attention and expectation conditions, with stronger associations when objects are unattended and in non-stimulus-driven voxels. This suggests pupil-linked arousal mechanisms contribute to overall V1 activity, potentially accounting for some of the stimulus-unspecific expectation suppression observed in V1.
evaluation: Claims C85-C86 demonstrate significant positive associations between pupil dilation and BOLD across conditions (all p≤0.005), with stronger effects when unattended (p=0.025). Claims C88-C89 show larger associations in non-stimulus-driven voxels (p=0.005). This supplemental analysis provides mechanistic insight into the stimulus-unspecific suppression in V1, supporting the interpretation that arousal-related global modulations contribute to expectation effects in early visual cortex. The evidence is robust and well-integrated with the main findings.

result: Baseline pupil size (measured before stimulus onset) does not differ between attention conditions or expectation conditions, indicating that pre-stimulus arousal levels are similar across conditions. This rules out baseline arousal differences as an explanation for the observed phasic pupil dilation differences.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 show no significant differences in baseline pupil size between conditions (both p>0.48, BFinclusion<0.26), with C92 interpreting this as evidence against baseline arousal differences. This control analysis is important for validating the interpretation of phasic pupil responses as reflecting stimulus-driven surprise rather than pre-existing arousal differences. The statistical evidence is clear and the Bayesian analyses support the null hypothesis.

result: The authors conclude that attention gates the integration of prior knowledge and sensory input, placing important constraints on neurocomputational theories that cast perceptual inference as automatic integration of prior and sensory information.
evaluation: These interpretive claims (C58-C59) are well-supported by the convergent evidence from multiple results: expectation suppression only occurs when stimuli are attended (despite equal learning and continued sensory processing when unattended), behavioral benefits only manifest with attention, and the dissociation between sensory and non-sensory regions. The theoretical implications are appropriately constrained and follow logically from the empirical findings. The conclusion challenges purely automatic accounts of predictive processing while remaining consistent with attention-gated predictive coding frameworks.

result: The study was preregistered with a target sample size of n=34 (powered to detect medium effects), recruited 38 participants, and excluded 4 following preregistered criteria (3 for excessive motion, 1 for incomplete data), resulting in the target sample size for analysis.
evaluation: These methodological claims (C78-C84) describe the study design, sample size justification, recruitment, and exclusions. The preregistration (C84) and adherence to preregistered exclusion criteria enhance the credibility of the findings. The sample size justification (C79) is appropriate for the primary analyses. The exclusion rate (~10.5%) is reasonable and the reasons are clearly documented. These methodological details support the rigor and transparency of the study.
